::: {.pageinfo}
A deep dive from [the clarinet's entry](index.qmd#clarinet) in post 3, which also covers [the flute](index.qmd#flute). Builds on [post 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd). Derivations are in folds. About 10 minutes. Written in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic's AI model.
:::

::: {.puzzle}
A clarinet and a flute are about the same length, yet the clarinet's lowest note is almost an [octave](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#octave) below the flute's. When players [overblow](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#overblow), the flute jumps up an octave and the clarinet an [octave and a fifth](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#octave). The same equation governs the air in both tubes. What is different?
:::

**The ends.** A flute is open at both ends; a clarinet is closed at the reed. A tube closed at one end fits a quarter of a wave where an open tube fits a half, so the same length sounds an octave lower and has modes only at the odd multiples of its lowest frequency. Hold the blow button on the clarinet, then switch the same tube to a flute and blow again. In the demo, the register key stands in for overblowing (on a flute, a faster, narrower airstream).

## The tube's equation {#operator}

Let $p(x, t)$ be the air pressure in the tube minus room pressure, at distance $x$ from the reed end of a tube of length $L$. Newton's law on a thin slab of air, together with the way air pushes back when squeezed, gives the string's [wave equation](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#wave-equation) again, now for the pressure (the [flute's entry](index.qmd#flute) derives it):
$$
\begin{gathered}
p_{tt} = -Ap, \qquad Ap = -c^2p_{xx}, \\
c^2 = \frac{K}{\rho} .
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $K$ is the air's [bulk modulus](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#bulk-modulus), its resistance to being squeezed, $\rho$ its density, and $c$ the speed of sound, about 343 m/s at 20 °C.[^speed]

The ends are part of the [operator](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#operator) $A$, and they are all that differ:

- **An open end** meets the room, so the pressure there is room pressure, $p = 0$, a [Dirichlet condition](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#dirichlet).[^pipes1] The flute has two: $p(0) = p(L) = 0$.
- **The clarinet's reed** is nearly shut, so the air there cannot move, and air that never moves feels no net push: the pressure has no slope, $p_x(0) = 0$, a [Neumann condition](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#neumann). Its bell is open, $p(L) = 0$.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The reed end, the end correction, and what the model leaves out</summary>

Let $\xi(x, t)$ be how far the air that normally sits at $x$ has moved along the tube. Newton's law on a slab is $\rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x$. At the reed the air cannot move, so $\xi = 0$ there at all times, so $\xi_{tt} = 0$, and Newton's law gives $p_x = 0$. The air just outside an open end moves with the air inside, so the tube acts slightly longer, by about 0.6 of its radius, an amount called the [end correction](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#end-correction) (J. Wolfe, [Pipes and harmonics](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/pipes.html), UNSW: "usually about 0.6 times the radius"). The model assumes a narrow cylindrical tube, small pressure changes and no friction at the walls. A real clarinet's bore is not exactly cylindrical, and its holes and bell matter; they refine the numbers below, not the picture (N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, [*The Physics of Musical Instruments*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-21603-4), 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapters 8 and 15).

</details>
:::

## Two tubes, two spectra {#spectrum}

The shapes the operator only stretches, $AX_n = \lambda_nX_n$, swing at $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi$. With the flute's ends they are the string's sines; with the clarinet's they are cosines that fit an odd number of quarter waves:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{flute:} && X_n = \sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}, \\
& && f_n = n\,\frac{c}{2L}, \\
&\text{clarinet:} && X_n = \cos\frac{(2n - 1)\pi x}{2L}, \\
& && f_n = (2n - 1)\,\frac{c}{4L} .
\end{aligned}
$$
The flute's modes sit at 1, 2, 3, 4, … times its lowest frequency, the clarinet's at 1, 3, 5, 7, … times its lowest,[^pipes2] and the clarinet's lowest, $c/4L$, is half the flute's, $c/2L$: an octave lower for the same length.[^fvc1]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The two spectra, step by step <span class="needs">derivatives</span></summary>

Writing $\lambda = c^2k^2$, the mode equation $-c^2X'' = \lambda X$ becomes $X'' = -k^2X$, solved by $X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx$, with $f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi = ck/2\pi$.

*Flute.* $X(0) = 0$ forces $a = 0$, and $X(L) = 0$ needs $\sin kL = 0$, so $kL = n\pi$: one half wave, two half waves, and so on. So $\lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2$ and $f_n = nc/2L$.

*Clarinet.* $X'(0) = bk = 0$ forces $b = 0$, leaving $X = \cos kx$, and $X(L) = 0$ needs $\cos kL = 0$, so $kL = (2n - 1)\pi/2$: one quarter wave, three quarter waves, and so on. So $\lambda_n = \big((2n - 1)\pi c/2L\big)^2$ and $f_n = (2n - 1)c/4L$.

As for the string, integration by parts rules out $\lambda \le 0$, and every pressure shape is a sum of these modes; the [appendix](../when-an-equation-has-a-spectrum/index.qmd#levels) says when such a sum is guaranteed.

</details>
:::

```{=html}
  <svg class="spec" id="cM4b" viewBox="0 0 320 96" style="max-width:520px" aria-label="The closed tube's modes: odd multiples of its lowest frequency only"></svg>
  <p class="cap">The tubes' modes, as multiples of each tube's lowest frequency: open at both ends (top), every line; closed at one end (bottom), the odd lines only. The stems mark where modes can sit; their heights carry no meaning here.</p>
```

[]{#what-we-hear}A real clarinet sounds a bit less than an octave below a flute, because the two differ a little in length, and the clarinet's mouthpiece and bell and the open ends change the effective length.[^fvc3]

## Blown: one repeating cycle {#sustained}

**A blown tube settles into one motion that repeats, close to one of its modes.** The clarinet's reed acts as a valve that the pressure in the mouthpiece opens and closes, so the air column drives the reed that feeds it.[^wolfe-clar1] On a flute, a jet of air blown across the embouchure hole does the reed's job.[^wolfe-flute1] Either way the result is a [self-sustained oscillation](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#self-sustained) ([appendix](../when-an-equation-has-a-spectrum/index.qmd#counterexamples)). It runs near one of the tube's modes, usually the lowest, with $L$ the tube up to the first open hole: the fingers choose the note by choosing $L$.

**The tube's modes pick the strong partials.** A sound that repeats has partials only at whole-number multiples of its repetition rate ([post 1](../what-you-hear/index.qmd#why-whole-numbers-repeat)), but it may have all of them. The tube's modes are odd multiples only, but its sound may have even ones too: in the low register the second and fourth harmonics are weak, since no mode of the tube supports them, and the first and third strong.[^wolfe-clar2] The breath sets the loudness and the brightness: blowing harder adds high harmonics.[^wolfe-clar3]

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <svg class="spec" id="cS4a" viewBox="0 0 320 96" style="max-width:520px" aria-label="The flute's blown sound: every whole-number multiple"></svg>
  <svg class="spec" id="cS4b" viewBox="0 0 320 96" style="max-width:520px" aria-label="The clarinet's blown sound: strong odd multiples, faint even ones"></svg>
  <p class="cap">The blown sounds, as multiples of the note being played: the flute (top) has every whole-number multiple; the clarinet (bottom) has strong odd multiples and faint even ones. The demos' sounds are made this way; the exact strengths are an illustrative choice.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

**The sound leaves through the open holes and the bell.** For most notes much of it leaves through the first open tone hole, the tube's effective open end; the bell radiates the lowest notes, and the high partials, which pass the open holes as if they were closed.[^cutoff] A flute also radiates from its embouchure hole, one of its two open ends. At an open end of area $S$ at $x = L$, the pressure slope pushes air in and out, and that pulsing flow is what the room hears: at a distance $R$ in open air, the sound is
$$
p_{\text{out}}(t) = -\frac{S}{4\pi R}\,p_x\Big(L,\ t - \frac{R}{c}\Big),
$$
So the room hears the frequencies of the air in the tube, in different amounts.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the formula for the sound comes from <span class="needs">derivatives</span></summary>

Let $v(t)$ be the outward speed of the air at the open end. Newton's law on the last thin slab of air is $\rho\,v_t = -p_x(L, t)$, so the volume of air flowing out each second, $U = Sv$, changes at the rate $U_t = -(S/\rho)\,p_x(L, t)$. An opening much smaller than the wavelength acts as a simple source, a small pulsating sphere, whose sound at a distance $R$ is $\rho\,U_t(t - R/c)/4\pi R$: it arrives $R/c$ seconds later and falls off as $1/R$ (N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, [*The Physics of Musical Instruments*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-21603-4), 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapters 7 and 8). Together these give the formula above. Mode $n$ enters $p_x(L, t)$ with an extra factor of its wavenumber $(2n - 1)\pi/2L$, so the open end favours the high partials. This is for one small opening radiating freely in all directions; with several open holes and the bell, the sound is a sum of such terms, one per opening.

</details>
:::

## Overblowing: a twelfth or an octave {#overblowing}

**The clarinet has no mode at twice its lowest frequency, so it overblows to three times.** When a clarinetist presses the register key, the tube jumps to its next mode, $3\times$ its lowest frequency: an octave and a fifth, called a twelfth.[^fvc2] A flutist overblows with a faster jet, and the flute's next mode is $2\times$ its lowest, an octave.[^wolfe-flute2]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>How the register key picks out the 3× mode</summary>

The register key opens a small hole, which for one low note lies a third of the way from the reed to the first open hole. An open hole pulls the pressure there toward room pressure, which spoils the fundamental, a mode that needs pressure variation at that point. For one note in the low register the hole sits right where that note's $3f_1$ mode has no pressure variation anyway, so the open hole does not disturb that mode. For the other notes the hole is off that point, and a second effect helps: the air in a small hole has mass, so the faster it must move back and forth, the harder it is to move. At the fundamental's lower frequency the hole leaks enough to spoil that mode; at the $3f_1$ mode's higher frequency it acts almost as a plug: "high frequency waves pass by as though it were closed". Either way the tube jumps to the $3f_1$ mode. (J. Wolfe, [Clarinet acoustics: an introduction](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/clarinetacoustics.html), UNSW)

</details>
:::

[^pipes1]: J. Wolfe, [Pipes and harmonics](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/pipes.html), UNSW: at an open end the "sound pressure (difference from atmospheric) is close to zero".
[^pipes2]: J. Wolfe, [Pipes and harmonics](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/pipes.html), UNSW: closed cylindrical bores "have only odd harmonics starting one octave lower".
[^fvc1]: J. Wolfe, [Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets)](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/flutes.v.clarinets.html), UNSW: for the same length, the closed pipe's lowest frequency "c/4L = 140 Hz – one octave lower than the flute".
[^fvc3]: J. Wolfe, [Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets)](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/flutes.v.clarinets.html), UNSW: "the lowest note on a clarinet is either the D or the C# below middle C", the flute's close to middle C; "There are complications due to end corrections", and the clarinet has a mouthpiece and "a flare and a bell".
[^wolfe-clar1]: J. Wolfe, [Clarinet acoustics: an introduction](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/clarinetacoustics.html), UNSW: "the reed acts like an oscillating valve".
[^wolfe-flute1]: J. Wolfe, [Flute acoustics: an introduction](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/fluteacoustics.html), UNSW: "The flutist blows a rapid jet of air across the embouchure hole"; "The flute is open at both ends."
[^wolfe-clar2]: J. Wolfe, [Clarinet acoustics: an introduction](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/clarinetacoustics.html), UNSW: "the sound spectrum in the low register has strong first and third harmonics, but weak second and fourth".
[^wolfe-clar3]: J. Wolfe, [Clarinet acoustics: an introduction](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/clarinetacoustics.html), UNSW: added harmonics make the sound brighter and louder; soft playing in the linear range gives "few high harmonics".
[^cutoff]: J. Wolfe, [Cutoff frequencies, crossfingering and half-holing in woodwinds](https://phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/cutoff.html), UNSW: below the tone holes' cutoff frequency a significant part of the power is radiated from the first open tone hole; "Above fc, a large fraction of the output sound is radiated from the bell." See also [Fletcher and Rossing](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-21603-4), chapter 15.
[^fvc2]: J. Wolfe, [Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets)](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/flutes.v.clarinets.html), UNSW: "the second register of the clarinet is a musical twelfth above the first".
[^wolfe-flute2]: J. Wolfe, [Flute acoustics: an introduction](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/fluteacoustics.html), UNSW: blowing harder or narrowing the lips gives "a faster jet", and the flute "jumps up" to the octave, $2f_1$.

```{=html}
(function () {

  var SEMIS = [11, 9, 7, 5, 4, 2]; // holes from the reed toward the bell
  var HOLES = SEMIS.map(function (s) { return LTOT * Math.pow(2, -s / 12); });
  var open = [false, false, false, false, false, false], reg = false, flute = false, voice = null;
  var FING = [{ n: "1", s: 0 }, { n: "2", s: 2 }, { n: "3", s: 4 }, { n: "4", s: 5 }, { n: "5", s: 7 }, { n: "6", s: 9 }, { n: "7", s: 11 }];
  function setFingering(s) { for (var i = 0; i < 6; i++) open[i] = s > 0 && SEMIS[i] <= s; update(); }
  function Leff() { for (var i = 0; i < 6; i++) if (open[i]) return HOLES[i]; return LTOT; }
  function modeN() { return reg ? 2 : 1; }
  function freq() { var L = Leff(); return flute ? modeN() * CSOUND / (2 * L) : (2 * modeN() - 1) * CSOUND / (4 * L); }
  function parts() { return C.models.clarinet.partials({ flute: flute }); }

  function freqFor(s) { var L = LTOT; for (var i = 0; i < 6; i++) if (s > 0 && SEMIS[i] <= s) { L = HOLES[i]; break; } return flute ? modeN() * CSOUND / (2 * L) : (2 * modeN() - 1) * CSOUND / (4 * L); }
  function labelFingerings() { FING.forEach(function (fg, i) { var nm = C.noteName(freqFor(fg.s)).name; FBTN[i].textContent = nm; FBTN[i].setAttribute("aria-label", "Fingering " + fg.n + ": " + nm); }); }

    osc.setPeriodicWave(C.wave(a, parts())); osc.frequency.value = freq();
    lp.type = "lowpass"; lp.frequency.value = flute ? 3500 : 4500;
    g.gain.setValueAtTime(0, t); g.gain.linearRampToValueAtTime(flute ? 0.4 : 0.3, t + 0.06);
    osc.connect(lp); lp.connect(g); g.connect(C.out); osc.start();
    voice = { osc: osc, g: g, lp: lp }; document.getElementById("blow").classList.add("on");
  }
  function stopBlow() {
    if (!voice) return; var t = C.ac().currentTime; voice.g.gain.cancelScheduledValues(t); voice.g.gain.setTargetAtTime(0, t, 0.04); voice.osc.stop(t + 0.4); voice = null;
    document.getElementById("blow").classList.remove("on");
  }
  function update() {

    var f = freq(), nn = C.noteName(f), L = Leff();
    labelFingerings();

    C.stems(document.getElementById("cSpec"), parts().slice(0, 12), { W: 320, H: 90, rmax: 12, fs: 8, sw: 2.5 });
  }
  var blow = document.getElementById("blow");
  blow.addEventListener("pointerdown", function (e) { e.preventDefault(); blow.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); startBlow(); });
  blow.addEventListener("pointerup", stopBlow); blow.addEventListener("pointercancel", stopBlow);

  window.addEventListener("keydown", function (e) {
    if (e.metaKey || e.ctrlKey || e.altKey || (e.target && e.target.tagName === "INPUT") || !mine(e)) return;
    e.preventDefault(); e.stopPropagation(); if (e.repeat) return;
    if (e.code === "Space") { startBlow(); return; }
    setFingering(FING[parseInt(e.key, 10) - 1].s);
  }, true);
  window.addEventListener("keyup", function (e) {
    if (!mine(e)) return; e.stopPropagation();
    if (e.code === "Space") stopBlow();
  }, true);
  var regB = document.getElementById("reg");
  regB.addEventListener("click", function () { reg = !reg; regB.setAttribute("aria-pressed", reg); update(); });
  function setType(fl) { flute = fl; document.getElementById("tClar").setAttribute("aria-pressed", !fl); document.getElementById("tFlute").setAttribute("aria-pressed", fl); update(); }
  document.getElementById("tClar").addEventListener("click", function () { setType(false); });
  document.getElementById("tFlute").addEventListener("click", function () { setType(true); });

  var cv = document.getElementById("pipe"), ctx = cv.getContext("2d");
  function geom() { var d = C.fit(cv), W = cv.width, H = cv.height, x0 = 30 * d, x1 = W - 16 * d; return { d: d, W: W, H: H, x0: x0, x1: x1, top: H * 0.32, bot: H * 0.68 }; }
  function X(g, L) { return g.x0 + (g.x1 - g.x0) * L / LTOT; }
  cv.addEventListener("pointerdown", function (e) {
    var r = cv.getBoundingClientRect(), g = geom(), px = (e.clientX - r.left) * g.d, best = -1, bd = 26 * g.d;
    HOLES.forEach(function (L, i) { var dx = Math.abs(X(g, L) - px); if (dx < bd) { bd = dx; best = i; } });
    if (best >= 0) { open[best] = !open[best]; update(); }
  });
  function draw(now) {
    var g = geom(), d = g.d, L = Leff(), xe = X(g, L), n = modeN();
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, g.W, g.H);
    var ph = C.reduce || !voice ? 1 : Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * 0.8 * now / 1000);
    for (var px = Math.floor(g.x0); px < g.x1; px += Math.max(1, Math.round(d))) {
      var xx = (px - g.x0) / (g.x1 - g.x0) * LTOT, amp;
      if (xx <= L) {
        var u = xx / L;
        amp = flute ? Math.sin(n * Math.PI * u) : Math.cos((2 * n - 1) * Math.PI * u / 2);
        var v = amp * ph, c = v >= 0 ? C.col["--pos"] : C.col["--neg"];
        ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb(c, Math.min(1, Math.abs(v)) * 0.85 + 0.05);
      } else ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--grid", 0.5);
      ctx.fillRect(px, g.top, Math.max(1, Math.round(d)), g.bot - g.top);
    }
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--ink"); ctx.lineWidth = 2 * d; ctx.strokeRect(g.x0, g.top, g.x1 - g.x0, g.bot - g.top);
    if (flute) { ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--paper"); ctx.fillRect(g.x0 - 2 * d, g.top + 2 * d, 4 * d, g.bot - g.top - 4 * d); }
    else { ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--ink"); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(g.x0, g.top); ctx.lineTo(g.x0 - 22 * d, (g.top + g.bot) / 2 - 3 * d); ctx.lineTo(g.x0 - 22 * d, (g.top + g.bot) / 2 + 3 * d); ctx.lineTo(g.x0, g.bot); ctx.closePath(); ctx.fill(); }
    HOLES.forEach(function (Lh, i) {
      var x = X(g, Lh), r = 9 * d;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(x, g.top - r - 6 * d, r, 0, 2 * Math.PI);
      if (open[i]) { ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--paper"); ctx.fill(); ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--ink"); ctx.lineWidth = 2 * d; ctx.stroke(); }
      else { ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--ink"); ctx.fill(); }
      ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); ctx.fillRect(x - 1 * d, g.top - 6 * d, 2 * d, 6 * d);
    });
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); ctx.lineWidth = 2 * d; ctx.setLineDash([4 * d, 4 * d]);
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(xe, g.top - 2 * d); ctx.lineTo(xe, g.bot + 14 * d); ctx.stroke(); ctx.setLineDash([]);
    ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); ctx.font = (11 * d) + "px 'IBM Plex Mono', monospace"; ctx.textAlign = "center";
    var lab = "sounding end", lw = ctx.measureText(lab).width, lx = Math.max(lw / 2 + 4 * d, Math.min(g.W - lw / 2 - 4 * d, xe));
    ctx.fillText(lab, lx, g.bot + 26 * d);
    ctx.textAlign = "left"; ctx.fillText(flute ? "open" : "reed", 4 * d, g.bot + 26 * d);
    requestAnimationFrame(draw);
  }
  C.onTheme(update);
  update(); requestAnimationFrame(draw);
})();
</script>
```

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, M = C.models;
  function modes(step) { var out = []; for (var n = 1; n <= 10; n += step) out.push({ ratio: n, amp: 1 }); return out; }
  function draw() {
    C.stems(document.getElementById("cM4a"), modes(1), { W: 320, H: 96, rmax: 10, fs: 8, sw: 3, noOff: true });
    C.stems(document.getElementById("cM4b"), modes(2), { W: 320, H: 96, rmax: 10, fs: 8, sw: 3, noOff: true });
    C.stems(document.getElementById("cS4a"), M.clarinet.partials({ flute: true }), { W: 320, H: 96, rmax: 10, fs: 8, sw: 3, noOff: true });
    C.stems(document.getElementById("cS4b"), M.clarinet.partials(), { W: 320, H: 96, rmax: 10, fs: 8, sw: 3, noOff: true });
  }
  C.onTheme(draw);
  draw();
})();
</script>
```
